newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - Jan 27.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - Jan 27.

text.p: The New York Times reported the following business stories on Monday:

* MEMC Electronic Materials' fourth quarter and year-end financial results could show the company topping $1 billion in annual revenes for the first time. The Missouri company is expected to report after the stock market closes on Monday.

* About 100 U.S. computer scientists are using the Very-High-Performance Backbone Network Service, an alternative Internet network built by MCI Communications linking the nation's five academic supercomputer centres.
* Nearly 4,100 workers at General Motors' plant in Ohio go on strike.

* Scientists at Xerox's research centre are working on micro-electro-mechanical systems, which may be used one day to allow highway overpasses to withstand earthquakes and to create self-repairing auto bumpers.
* A group of scientists, including researchers at Xerox, plans to announce today the creation of a microscopic magnet that would make computing thousands of times faster.
* Television news in Australia is a battle ground for high ratings, with networks owned by Rupert Murdoch and Kerry Packer among the contenders.
* The personal computer industry shipped 70.9 million machines in 1996, up 17.8 percent from 1995, according to market research group Dataquest.
* Companies using snazzy special effects in Super Bowl advertising include Royal Appliance Manufacturing, which showed Fred Astaire dancing with one of its vacuum products.
* Advertising companies target New Year's resolutions to pull in customers for their clients.
* Many films shown at the Sundance Film Festival may never be released, even though a number of high-profile acquisitions have taken place at the festival.
* New web sites accompany the re-release of the "Star Wars" film by News Corp's Twentieth Century Fox Home Entertainment.

* U.S. states have plenty of cash after five years of economic growth, but rather than quickly spending the money as in past periods of economic boom, they are holding onto their funds in preparation for the next business decline.
